title: Observation-trained machine learning halves estimated Arctic winter sea-ice surface cooling
summary: A neural network trained on observations from five Arctic field campaigns reduced ERA5 errors in the Arctic sea-ice surface energy budget and removed ERA5’s wintertime near-surface warm bias of about 4 K. The corrected estimates imply about 50% weaker winter surface cooling and 80–120 cm seasonal thermodynamic ice growth, closer to SMOS–CryoSat thickness increases than ERA5’s 150–200 cm estimate.
organization: Alfred Wegener Institute; Helmholtz Centre Hereon; Helmholtz AI; Deutsches Klimarechenzentrum; NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory; University of Leeds; Norwegian Polar Institute; Karlsruhe Institute of Technology; Stockholm University; Washington State University

evidence.tested: A neural network trained on observations from five Arctic field campaigns reduced ERA5 errors in the Arctic sea-ice surface energy budget and removed ERA5’s wintertime near-surface warm bias of about 4 K.
evidence.unknown: Validation uses leave-one-campaign-out cross-validation and multiple field campaigns, but direct flux observations remain sparse in space and time. The climatology applies to ice-covered Arctic regions north of 70°N with sea-ice concentration above 80%; authors do not recommend extrapolation to marginal ice zones or coastal regions. The ice-growth values are thermodynamic estimates rather than direct pan-Arctic measurements.
evidence.ai_role: The network learned the relationship between ERA5 atmospheric states and observed fluxes from MOSAiC, SHEBA, AO2018, N-ICE2015 and ARTofMELT campaigns, then bias-corrected hourly Arctic sea-ice surface fluxes for 1994–2024 to derive a revised regional climatology and ice-growth estimates.
